title: Visitor pattern
idea: The Visitor pattern adds new operations to a fixed set of classes by putting each operation in a visitor object with one method per class.
points: Each element's `accept` calls back the visitor method for its own type.
Two calls choose the code: element type, then visitor type. That is double dispatch.
New operations are cheap; a new element type forces edits in every visitor.
The JDK's `Files.walkFileTree` takes a `FileVisitor` with one callback per event.

messages.label: accept(eval)
messages.note: The caller holds only an `Expr`. It does not know the node is a `Mul`.

messages.label: visitMul(this)
messages.note: `Mul` knows its own type, so it calls the matching visitor method.

messages.label: left.accept(this)
messages.note: The visitor recurses into the left child and passes itself along.

messages.label: visitAdd(this)
messages.note: `Add` routes back to `visitAdd`. No `instanceof`, no cast.

messages.label: accept(this)
messages.note: Each `Num` leaf answers through `visitNum` with its own value.

messages.label: result
messages.note: `visitMul` multiplies both child results and returns the product to the caller.

code.title: The problem: overloads
code.caption: Overloads look like per-type dispatch, but Java picks them from the declared type.

walk.text: Three overloads. It looks as if Java will choose one per node type.
`e` is declared `Expr`, so the compiler binds `print(Expr)` for every element.
Even if `print(Add)` ran, its children are typed `Expr`, so each child would print `?`.
The usual workaround is an `instanceof` chain, repeated in every operation.
A forgotten node type is caught only at runtime, by this throw.

code.title: The fix: visitors
code.caption: Each node routes to the right visitor method; each operation is one class.

walk.text: One method per element type. Distinct names avoid any overload confusion.
`sealed` fixes the element set: only these three records may implement `Expr`.
Each `accept` is one line: call the visitor method for my own type.
`EvalVisitor` recurses with `accept(this)`; the exact-math calls throw on overflow.
A second operation is one new class. No element class changed.
One tree, two operations, chosen by which visitor you pass in.

pitfalls: Passing an `Expr` variable to overloaded `visit` methods skips type dispatch; go through `accept`.
Choosing Visitor while element types still change often means editing every visitor each time.
Visitors that need private element data push you to add getters; check encapsulation first.

quiz.q: A tree has three node types and four visitors. You add a `Neg` node. What must change?
quiz.why: `Neg` needs a `visitNeg` method in `Visitor`, and every visitor then fails to compile until it implements it. New element types are Visitor's costly direction.

takeaway: Visitor makes new operations cheap and new element types expensive.
